utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-97-25-T, the Prosecutor versus Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Before we resume with the witness, there's a problem next Wednesday in relation to the availability of the room where the videolink is coming from, and the suggestion is that we start with FWS-49 rather than with 137 so that we can have the videolink evidence taken, and then we can resume hearings with the witness here. Is there any problem with that from the Prosecutor's point of view?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any problem from the Defence point of view?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. The next problem is that the room which is to be used for the videolink testimony is not going to be available until 10.00 in the morning, so it seems to me the best idea would be to start the proceedings at 10.00 and run everything half an hour later than usual, provided there's no problems from the interpreters, the court reporters, or the audio/videolink people. If there are any, please let us know. Right, well, we'll resume.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: As we are already talking about the witness order, we have to announce that the witness 210 could not arrive here. He still has problems with his passport, so we will not have this witness next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right, then. Do we need another one to fill in, or are we so far behind with the list at the moment that you don't need one?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We are far behind, and we -- actually, we cannot replace him because we don't have any more witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So, we have to -- he will then be our last witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And he'll be here the following week, will he?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, it's good to see the end in sight. Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise for interrupting. There is one thing I did not understand and which would be important for the Defence. What did you mean, that 210 would come next week or the week after next? The translation I heard was that 210 was due next week, or is it impossible for 210 to come next week and Witness 210 will then come the week after that? This is important for Defence planning, so I apologise for interrupting, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That is all right, Mr. Bakrac. What was said was that 210 cannot be here next week so he'll be here the week after. So we'll have only 210, hopefully, the week after next, and there will be the rest of that week and then two more weeks for you to be able to prepare your Defence, but we will have to have a Pre-Trial Conference at some stage, probably at the end of that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Let's go on with the witness. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I have a few more questions for you. I would like you to look at document P240/7, and document ID 240/6. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In document 240/7 under number 127 is the name Music, Stevan -- Music, Enes, father's name, Nazif. On document 240/6 under number 59, the same person's name is mentioned, Music, Enes, father's name, Nazif. In document ID 240/6 it says that he was born in 1922, while in document P240/7 it says that this person was born on the 23rd of May, 1970. Can you please explain to us - because as you said, you drafted document 240/6 on the basis of document 240/7 - is it one and the same person; and if it is one and the same person, how come the dates of birth are quite different?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you said is correct. In our list, his year of birth is 1922, and in the list that was compiled by the Serb prison authorities, on the basis of which document 240/7 was drafted, it says that he was born in 1970. In our records, his date of birth is 1922, and we drew on our own records. I assume that it is the same person, but I do allow for the possibility of another person with the same name and surname to exist. However, it is hard to believe that everything coincides, the prisoner's name, surname and father's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now I would like to ask you to look at 240/5 in addition to 240/7. In document 240/5 under number 14, the name of Berber, Enver, is written there, born in 1957; in 240/7 under number 11 is the name of Berder, Enver, born on the 1st of January, 1937. Is this one and the same person? If it is one and the same person, how do you explain this difference in dates of birth?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is one and the same person. There is no surname like "Berder" in the territory of the former Yugoslavia or Bosnia-Hercegovina, let alone the Foca region. There is the last name of Berber only. So perhaps the prison authorities, when compiling this list that they handed over to the International Red Cross, they consciously or subconsciously made a mistake. This is not the only mistake in this list. There are also some other mistakes in the designation of surnames. However, as in the previous case, as the date of birth, the year of birth, we mentioned the year that is recorded in our files. I think, but I cannot say for sure, that in the book of the International Red Cross it says that this person's name is Berber, Enver, and that the year of birth matches the one that we have in our own records. This can be checked in the book, the register of the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In view of your answer, I would like to ask you to look at document ID 240/6 which you drafted, rather, the state commission did. In it, under item 5, is Berber, Enver, born in 1937, like in document P240/7. A few minutes ago you said that when compiling 240/5, you used your own records; however, from this we can see that it matches what is in document 240/7. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. Obviously this was a slip of the tongue in the previous document. Actually, could you repeat what you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Number five.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, number five.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Number five in document ID 240/6, his date of birth is identical to that in number 11 in document 240/7, and it differs from the date of birth in document P240/5.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document of ours was compiled on the basis of the previous document in which it says that the person was born in 1937, that is to say, on the basis of the document of the International Red Cross committee. However, I believe, and it is possible to check this out in the register of the International Red Cross, that his year of birth is 1957 rather than 1937, as the document sent by the prison authorities to the International Red Cross says.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you be quite sure that it is one and the same person?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be absolutely certain; however, since the father's name and the name and surname of the person concerned are the same, I believe that it is one and the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In list P240/7 under number 22, the name of Brkovic, Hasan, is listed, born in 1938. In list P240/5, it says that Hasan Brkovic was born in 1939. Is it one and the same person, and how do you explain the discrepancy in the years of birth?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that in the document that was compiled by the prison authorities and on the basis of which this document was compiled by the International Committee of the Red Cross, there is a number of mistakes that were made in these documents in terms of names and dates of birth. In this case, I assume that the date -- or rather, the year of birth that we have in our records of the state commission is correct rather than the date that was given by the prison authorities to the International Committee of the Red Cross. If you take a look at this, you'll see in the document of the prison authorities it is only the year of birth that is mentioned and that the date and month have not been included. May I explain? These errors in the document of the International Red Cross, in a few cases, either when these documents were sent from the prison authorities or when the documents were translated into the English language, there were certain typographical errors that were made in the case of names. And I can give you a few such errors that we managed to detect, either when the prison authorities typed these names out or when this was translated into the English language. There are some names there that do not exist in Bosnia and Herzegovina at all. Sometimes the error involves one letter and sometimes even more than that, but it affects either the name and/or the surname of the detainee.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: As you said, you had not seen this document of the prison authorities which was later translated into English.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never had the opportunity of seeing the original document of the prison authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I don't think I should go into all the 11 discrepancies between documents 240/7 and 240/5. Can you confirm that in all 11 cases it is one and the same person that is involved, and that it is only a question of years of birth that were not registered properly; or should I mention each of these 11 names individually to you?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this possibility, that there are different persons involved, is only in the realm of theory. I am convinced that all the persons mentioned in the list of the International Red Cross and those who were noted by us are actually the same people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, whilst I accept that that is the witness's honest belief, it's a matter for us to determine in the end as to whether they're the same people. I would prefer that you did draw attention to those discrepancies where they are of some significance in the case so that the witness has a chance to answer them; otherwise, we are in difficulty ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour. I'm just trying to see whether the persons are the same because the discrepancies are up to 40 or 50 years, even; and after all, it was the commission that made up these lists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Of course this is not the only evidence we have about any of this material, but nevertheless, if there are significant discrepancies, I suggest you put them to the witness for him to explain. It may be the same explanation each time, in which case the witness can say, "This is the same as the last one." But I think we should have them because I don't want them to be raised for the first time in your final addresses when we've no longer got the witness here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Then I'll take them one at a time and I'll move according to the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The next name is under item 37 in document 240/5, Cengic, Bilal, born in 1946 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure about the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Can we have that year again, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1956.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: 1956, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: This person in document 240/7 under the same name is registered as being born on the 1st of January, 1976.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In most cases where the International Red Cross did not have the precise day and month of birth, they put the 1st of January or they avoided any mention, so they would just put zero zero day, zero zero month, and then the year of birth. As for the discrepancy between the years of birth, my answer is the same as it was before: I am convinced that our records are correct rather than the information provided by the prison authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, I don't want to seem disrespectful, but it's for us to determine that and not you. That may be your belief, but for us to determine it, we have to know why you are so convinced. Now, if there is an explanation which leads you to be so convinced, will you please give it to us so we can then determine for ourselves whether or not these are the same people. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I do have an explanation. This document which, in my opinion, abounds in discrepancies or errors, was compiled by the prison authorities, consciously or subconsciously. Perhaps they were even trying to present the detainees as being younger than they actually were. Our records, however, of the state commission are based on a larger number of sources, and the most important sources are the family members themselves. I have to believe that if a son reports about his father, that the son gives the father's exact date of birth. That is why I believe that our records are more accurate than those compiled by the prison authorities. I wish to point out that family members are not the only source of information. During the first day of my testimony, I think that I mentioned that we also mentioned the statistics database of the consensus that was made in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1991, the last one was, and the information there is very accurate: name, surname, father's name, the so-called identification number of every adult person, and date of birth. So on the basis of all of this, I believe that our records are correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: May I put this to you, because I only want to make sure we come to the right conclusion in this case: You may have the right details about the father of the son who reports that his father is missing, but we have to be satisfied that his father was in the KP Dom. Now, it may very well be you've got the right identification for somebody who may not have been in the KP Dom. Now, what did you do to check that the person being reported by the son in this particular case was the person who had been in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about this earlier. In our list of 266 persons that are considered to be missing from the KP Dom, who were last seen at the KP Dom, that list was compiled on the basis of certification from at least two independent sources. In certain cases, we even had four completely independent sources that confirmed the presence of precisely these persons in the KP Dom Foca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Number 54, document 240/5, there's the name of Dervisevic, Fadil, born in 1964. Number 47, document P240/7, it says that Dervisevic, Fadil, was born on the 27th of January, 1969.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is the same as it was in response to your previous question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Item 59 -- Duric, Ahmo, is mentioned born in 1964, and under item number 51 under document P240/7 Duric, Ahmo, was born in 1972.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is the same as it was in response to your previous question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Item 106 in document 240/5, Jahic, Bego, born in 1969; and in 83, document 240/7, it says that Jahic, Brgo, was born on the 1st of January, 1960. There is even a difference in the surname.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only the surname. If you looked at it carefully, if you analysed this document, you could see that even the father's name was misspelled. So we checked this information of Jahic, Bego, son of Murif - not as Murip as the prison authority said here - and the date of birth, the year of birth, is not the one that was reported by the prison authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In document 240/6 under number 41, it really says Jahic, Bego, son of Murif. You say you corrected the father's name. Why didn't you correct the year of birth, too, because in this document it also says that he was born in 1960.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand you. Is there a difference between our records and the records of the International Red Cross as submitted by the prison authorities, that is, in terms of the year of birth?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said to us a few minutes ago that in relation to document P240/7, that, as you said, was given to the Red Cross by the prison authorities. In document 240/6, which you compiled on your own on the basis of the previous document, you corrected the information provided for Jahic, Bego. You corrected his name and his father's name in relation to the report of the prison authorities. I'm asking you now, why you did not correct in that document the year of birth, too, 1960 into 1969, as you did in 240/5?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understood the question. In this list, which was compiled on the basis of an analysis of the list of the International Committee of the Red Cross, it obviously should have said "Murip," which was the wrong name of the father as mentioned by the prison authorities. It is only in our list, in the list of 266 persons, it was supposed to say Jahic, Bego, son of Murif, the year of birth, 1969.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So in this case, in document 240/6, you made only partial corrections, not entire?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We corrected only the father's name from Murip to Murif.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And the name of the victim from Brgo to Bego, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Considering that in document 240/5 we don't have the father's name - there is no such column - is this the same person?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please tell me the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Number 106.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it is one and the same person, Bego Jahic, born in 1969. This person does not come from the Foca municipality originally. He was arrested in the Republic of Montenegro and was then deported and turned over to Serbian authorities on the border of Bosnia and Herzegovina and taken to the KP Dom Foca where he was last seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In line 106 of document 240/5 which we've just mentioned, in the column indicating "former residence in 1991," this space is empty. Can Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you please tell us why it is empty? The former residence of this person in 1991 is not indicated.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This man was born in Srebrenica, but we were unable to determine his residence in April 1992 or in 1991, but we know for a fact that he was born in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In document 240/6 - which you prepared based on, as you say, document 240/7 - in line 41, Bego Jahic, father's name, Murif, it says that he was born in 1960 in Kozja Luka. Is that on the territory the Foca municipality?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not clear which document he's referring to. 240/6 contains 90 names, and that's the one which the witness prepared -- oh, sorry, my mistake, Your Honour, he's referring to 240/7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's right. It's exactly the same concession the witness made earlier. You proceed, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, in document 240/6, which you prepared and based on document 240/7, in line 41 it says Bego Jahic, father's name Murif, born in 1960, last residence, Kozja Luka, Pirni Do. Is Kozja Luka on the territory of Foca municipality?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I suppose you're talking about Pirni Do. That is one of the local communes on the territory of the municipality of Foca, and we were able to determine, based on certain testimonies, that this person was either employed or had in-laws, I cannot be precise, on the territory of Foca municipality. What is indubitable is that he was not born on the territory of Foca municipality but in Srebrenica, and that he was deprived of liberty in Montenegro. That much is known precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If it is indeed the same person as in line 106 of document 240/5, why was this information about the residence of Pirni Do not included by you in the other table for the person Bego Jahic?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, we are not sure that Bego Jahic in April 1992, at the moment of outbreak of the conflict, resided on the territory of Foca municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Based on what, then, did you, in line 41 of document 240/6, did you write "Kozja Luka, Pirni Do"?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was based on the testimony of a witness with whom we had worked immediately before the preparation of this list in an effort to make the list complete because we didn't have complete information in all cases for this list which we provided to the OTP. And if necessary, I can tell you the name of this witness who provided us with this information to the effect that this man had some sort of shelter or a safe residence. Not permanent residence, but some sort of residence on the territory of Foca municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the name of that witness?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Preljub Avro [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction, Tafro.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can we then conclude that in your document which you prepared, 240/6, in line 41 regarding Bego Jahic, father's name Murif, you corrected the name of the victim, the name of the father; you inserted the last residence in 1991; and you left intact only the year of birth as 1960 as indicated in document 240/7?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last name and the victim's year of birth are the same as in document 240/7. The name is changed from Brgo to Bego, one letter is changed, therefore; and the father's name is changed from Murip to Murif, also a change of one letter, and we did that because it was obvious that it was a typographical error made either by the prison authorities or the person who translated this into English and was not familiar with the names and surnames common in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In line 130 of document 240/5, Esad Kovacevic, it says he was born in 1963; and in document 240/7 under number 98, Esad Kovacevic is said to have been born in 1953.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same as my previous answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Under number 175 of document 240/5, Enes Music --

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've also discussed this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Under number 177, document 240/5, Amir Stevanovic [as interpreted] --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The year of birth is indicated as 1972. And under number 121, there is Amil Musanovic, the year of birth is 1st January 1968, and that is in document 240/7. There is a discrepancy in the names and the years of birth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Before you answer that, sir. Mr. Vasic, the interpreters did not hear clearly the name that you read from document 177 -- I'm sorry, document 240/5, the first version of that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. In document 240/5, number 177, there is Amir Musanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And then what is the second name that you read?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second name in document 240/7 is Amil, with an L, Musanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So it's the given name that changes in each case, but the family name is the same. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no difference here. If you look closely at number 176, you will see that it says Amil Musanovic, born 1968, as indicated in document 240/7.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I would agree with you, but you would then have to clarify how come that in document 240/6, which you prepared based on document 240/7, there is no such name as Amil Musanovic, but instead, under number 63 [as interpreted] there is Amir, with an R, Musanovic, born in 1968?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's possible that a mistake has been made here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And in number 178 in document 240/5 there is an Edhem Musanovic, born 1955; whereas in document 240/7 in line 122, Ethem, with a T, Musanovic, the year of birth is 1963 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Your Honour, the transcript says 1963, and the year of birth was actually 1933. That is page 16, line 17, at the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is the same as in response to your previous questions. There is a difference in one letter, that is, between Edhem and Ethem, and a difference in the year of birth. That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Is the person's name really Edhem or Ethem?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the name is actually with a D, Edhem.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In line 61, document 240/6, prepared by you based on document 240/7, there is really a name Edhem Musanovic, and the year of birth 1933. Why, when you were correcting the name of this person, didn't you also correct his year of birth, as you did in document 240/5?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why this hasn't been done. I can only say for sure that the name is Edhem, and the correct year of birth is the one stated in our document, on our records.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow me, I would like to say one thing. The document that we prepared, 240/6, does not exist in our computer database as such. We were only requested by the Office of the Prosecutor to make an analysis of the document of the International Red Cross, and it is possible that the person who did this analysis according to my instructions made corrections of the names, surnames, father's names in those cases where our records contained correct information, whereas the years of birth were simply taken over from the document given to us by the Red Cross in the form of document 240/7. And it is therefore possible that the names are corrected in our document 240/6, whereas years of birth were simply copied from the ICRC's document. I cannot state this for a fact, but I assume that is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, please, what is the purpose of your instructions to make such partial corrections relating only to names and father's names without correcting the years of birth?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't give any such instructions. I instructed the person to make this analysis of the document, and it is obvious that our database contains only correct names. And when the person was doing the analysis, the -- they just copied the dates of birth from the document given to us by the Red Cross. This original document, 240/6, does not exist as such. It is just an analysis of the document originally prepared by the prison authorities and handed over to us by the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Of course, sir, I suppose that the purpose of preparing this document was to help my colleagues from the Prosecutor in listing the potential victims, but we will move on. Number 138 [as interpreted], document 240/5, Mehmedalija Sljivo, born in 1966; and in line 151 in document 240/7, Mehmedalija Sljivo is said to have been born in 1964. Shall I repeat it?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 238 of the document 240/5. It says here in the transcript 138. I didn't understand you quite. I think there must be a mistake in the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'll repeat my question to make things clear. Item 238 of the document 240/5 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, the court reporters are complaining about the speed with which you're reading these documents. You've got to remember that this is fairly complicated stuff to translate and to type with names and dates and things. It's not like the usual form of question and answer, so please slow down.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is the same as in response to your previous question. You will notice in the records of the prison authorities that there is no full date of birth; no day or month, only the year of birth is indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, we have gone over the discrepancies between documents 240/5 and 240/7 regarding names and years of birth of victims. Could you please tell us, you said that the report 240/7 abounds with imprecisions; however, this report contains 184 items and there are discrepancies in years of birth and names in only 11 cases. Can you agree with me it is hardly appropriate to use the words "abounds with"?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You misquoted me again. I didn't say that it abounded with imprecisions. I rather said that there is a number of errors in that list. The words "abounds with" would mean that it is full of mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And could you please tell me with regard to these lists why, when you were using all this information from the report 240/7, you didn't use also the date of notification when you were filling in the rubric month of disappearance for the persons listed in document 240/5?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all these cases which refer to the KP Dom Foca, the date of notification is the same: 30th of August, 1992. If you go through this document, you will see that in all cases where the prison in Foca is concerned, the date is always the same: 30th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I can hardly agree with you, sir. For instance, in item 1, document 240/7, the date of notification is 17th June 1974 [as interpreted]. In item 5, this date of notification is 15th of August, 1993. In item 6, the date is 31st of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. If you allow me to answer before you go on enumerating all the dates; you did not hear me out quite. I said in all cases where the Foca prison is concerned. You just mentioned some other prisons, not the Foca prison. With regard to other prisons, the dates of notification are those when other prisons, not Foca but Trnopolje, Kula, Sarajevo, Doboj, and perhaps some other prisons made the notification. But if you look at the items where the prison concerned is Foca, you will see that the date is always the same: The 30th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, in document 240/7, item 137, it says that the person detained in Foca prison, the date of notification is 15th of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right, but in this case our analysis didn't show that this person is missing. This person was released or, rather, exchanged. This person is alive and well, thank God.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. During your testimony you mentioned that as you cooperated with the Commission for Missing Persons of the Republika Srpska, that you realised that some ethnic Serbs were detained by the army of the federation. Do you know how many Serbs were detained in these prisons?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether I can be very accurate, but the largest number of prisoners, prisoners of war, are from 1994 and 1995; that is to say, at the time when the legal authorities, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Croat Defence Council did achieve some success in the battlefield in Mount Vlasic, Ozren, Majevica, near Tuzla. At that time in the prisons in Tuzla and Sarajevo -- and yes, of course, I didn't mention the front line at Bihac and Bosanski Krajina. At that time there were a large number of prisoners of war coming into these prisons. So throughout the war, these prisoners of war were being released, so it is hard to say. If I were to assess what the largest number of prisoners of war was at one point in time, I don't think that this figure ever exceeded 1200, perhaps a bit more than that. Perhaps a bit more.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: How many of these persons went missing?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the records of the International Red Cross, I think that the number of Bosnian Serbs that spent more or less time in government prisons does not exceed -- I think that it does not exceed the number of ten. Perhaps it's not even that much. I'm talking about the number of prisoners. The number of Bosnian Serbs that continued to be missing during the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina is considerably higher.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the examination-in-chief, you said that your records included civilians. On which basis did you come to the conclusion that these were civilians only when you were compiling documents P240/5 and document -- and the document on missing persons from the municipality of Foca, since in some cases of exhumations a number of persons, a small number of persons, that is, were found wearing olive-green/grey trousers or olive-green/grey socks?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already pointed out that these records include civilian persons only. As for the municipality of Foca, military losses are over 700 men who were engaged in the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the records we have here today refer to civilian persons only. It is easy to explain the circumstances. You put it quite well, that there's actually a negligible number of people who were found wearing military boots. In a few cases there are also persons who were wearing military trousers. But that can be easily explained. People used what they had at hand. You have to realise that there was no transportation, that people primarily went on foot and in such terrain that wore out their shoes quickly, so military boots were the kind of footwear that was best suited for such conditions. On the basis of what I know about exhumations in the territory of Foca, I think, as far as I know, that there weren't more than five cases when persons were found wearing parts of military clothing or footwear, just parts. So I don't think that in any case we exhumed a person that was wearing full military gear, that is to say, clothing and footwear. In a vast majority of cases, if you are to analyse the police reports, you will see that they are wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. During your examination-in-chief, you mentioned that a person registered in document P55, that is List C in the indictment, was Mujezinovic, Omir, number 18, was killed in a car accident. Can you tell us when this person was killed in a car accident?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we analysed this list, we found it strange that Mujezinovic, Omir, was not in our records and was on this list. We assumed that the Prosecutor has some evidence about this, that this person was at the KP Dom. And as we tried to find out whether Omir Mujezinovic exists at all, we found out that he was killed before the war in a car accident. We do not know whether there is another person by the name of Omir Mujezinovic. We think that this is Samir Mujezinovic who was really at the KP Dom and who is considered to be missing from the KP Dom and who has been registered as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you check about Omir Mujezinovic outside the territory of the Foca, like Gorazde, Visegrad, Bileca?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there were detainees at the KP Dom coming from these areas as well?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that in 1992, a number of persons from Montenegro were brought to the KP Dom in 1992, persons who did not reside in Foca before that. Gorazde, Srebrenica. I am not sure whether there are some other municipalities. Oh, yes, the municipality of Kalinovik. A certain number of persons were brought in, either from Montenegro or from these municipalities -- parts of these municipalities, rather, that were under Serb force control. They were brought to the KP Dom at Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During your examination-in-chief, you said, you said that Foca was a black hole. That was the expression you used. However, from the exhumation reports which I presume you handed over to my colleagues at the OTP, and I got it from them, I believe that you were assisted when you were obtaining various reports from Republika Srpska, primarily by a person from the commission that dealt in such matters in Republika Srpska, and also the assistance of the police. And I see that you also enjoyed the assistance of international forces. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only the assistance, I would say that we had very decent cooperation with the local police and administration. However, I said that Foca, until a year or two ago, had been a black hole. It indeed had been that way. It was inconceivable a year or two ago to get into the town of Foca. We could move about the outskirts of the municipality of Foca, and we could carry out exhumations there because there was less danger. There wasn't any local population. These were not populated areas at all. But the closer we got to the urban area of Foca, the situation became increasingly difficult. During my testimony, I have already pointed out that the representatives of international forces of SFOR and IPTF advised us to refrain from exhumations in Foca and around Foca. You have to know that it was only last year, I think, and this is eight years after the liquidation of the victims and a full five years after the peace agreement was signed for Bosnia, that we managed to enter the town of Foca. The situation was similar in the municipality of Visegrad. Before, the situation in Bratunac was similar as well. But Srebrenica was different. Our teams managed to get in as early as 1996 and to do their job. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I see that the exhumation reports show that some exhumations were carried out by your commission in 1997. Actually, your commission attended them.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the first exhumations in the territory of the municipality of Foca were carried out as far back as 1996; however, in that part of the municipality of Foca which now belongs to the federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say, which the Dayton peace accords separated it as belonging to the federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In 1997, we carried out an exhumation in Previla, and as I said yesterday, I think that Previla belongs to the federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was only in the later years and most intensively last year and at the end of 1999 and mid-1999 that we slowly started approaching the urban areas of Foca municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know whether in the period before 1999 the Commission for Tracing Missing Persons of Republika Srpska carried out some exhumations in the territory of the federation; for example, where there is information that there are Serb victims?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far back as mid-1996. Our colleagues from Republika Srpska came to the territory of the federation to the site of Mount Ozren, to be precise, where I think 66 Serb soldiers were exhumed. Those who were killed in combat action during the summer of 1995 when the government forces took the area of Mount Ozren.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about civilians? Were such exhumations carried out?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is an ongoing process. As I speak here, it is quite possible that our colleagues from Republika Srpska are carrying out exhumations of war victims right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Tell me, bearing in mind the situation that you mentioned that currently prevails in the municipality of Foca and that there is full cooperation, are there any legal obstacles for the return of ethnic Muslims to this area? You mentioned that during your examination-in-chief; you talked about the return of such persons.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there are no legal obstacles. There are obstacles of a different nature. People have no place to return to. Somewhat over 11.000 dwellings existed in the territory of Foca, over 4.800 were destroyed, and several thousand were totally destroyed. So their houses were damaged or destroyed, and their livestock was taken away or killed. That goes for the rural population, whereas the urban population also has no place to return to, and their children would have to study a history that does not involve their own people. So we can say objectively speaking that not only the territory of Foca, but also throughout Republika Srpska and throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina there are significant obstacles in the path of the return of persons who wish to go back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have only two more questions. During the proceedings before this honourable Trial Chamber, the question arose of what the abbreviation AID means, A-I-D? Can you help us in this record? What is this organisation involved in, the organisation with whose name is abbreviated as A-I-D?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with the abbreviation, and its full name is the Agency for Investigations and Documentation. I think it was established after the peace agreement was signed in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was established by the highest state authority, the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I'm not sure whether I am familiar with the details involved in their work. I can say that from time to time we obtain information from this agency in relation to this particular part, pertaining to the state commission, that is to say, that if they learn in the course of their activity that there are individual or mass graves somewhere, they are duty-bound, and not only them, but all other state authorities - courts, attorneys, the police - they have to inform the state commission thereof. This is written down in the regulations pertaining to the work of the state commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you receive information from this commission which becomes accessible to them from witness statements?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of the sources of their information. I don't think that they reveal them, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether you know who finances this organisation, this agency?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I absolutely do not know what are the sources of its financing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: My last question has to do with a TV programme that was shown on Sarajevo television last year and has to do with the work of this commission, and do you know whether that it was mentioned on the 9th of September, 1992, in Koviljaca on the Drina River an exchange was not carried out because you did not agree to have this exchange carried out between your side and the Serb side? Is that information correct as broadcast on this TV programme?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am really not aware of that. I did not watch this programme. There have been quite a few programmes in Bosnia-Herzegovina and abroad about the work of this state commission. On the 20th of August, as I mentioned, in 1992 I became a member of the State Commission for Tracing Missing Persons, but I think that since that you already mentioned the name of this particular site, this site certainly cannot be on the Drina River. At that time, the Drina River was totally controlled by the Serb forces. There was no separation line there, so I'm not aware of that. There is a site that has a somewhat different name than the one you referred to. That is the site of Koviljaca and that is near Sarajevo. But I am not aware of the event that you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know the name of Kasim Dranka [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just warn you that there is a typing mistake here. It's not Dranka, it's Trnka, which is T-r-n-k-a. I know the name. This is a prominent professor from Sarajevo. He was also my professor at the time when I studied law. For a long time he was our ambassador, the ambassador of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia. After that, he was advisor to one of the members of the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's what I know about the gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence has no further questions for Mr. Masovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Re-examination, Mr. Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Masovic. Just a couple of questions in relation to document 240/7. This is the document received by you at a working committee conducted by the Red Cross, and it relates to the detainees notified by the army of the Republika Srpska to the Red Cross authorities as to people detained in their facilities. You mentioned that you received the -- this version of the document that we have in court today in English from a representative of the Red Cross. Did the representative say to you or to anyone at that meeting as to how they were notified by the army of the Republika Srpska as to Bosnian Muslims being detained in their detention centres on the document? Did they say whether these notifications that appear on the document were in writing by the authorities, or were they oral, over the telephone or in person?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already pointed out that in the terminology that is used in the work of the working group, we constantly refer to the prison authorities of one or the other or the third side. So we did not talk about the army of Republika Srpska or the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the terminology that we use; we always talk about prison authorities. Even nowadays when we talk to the representatives of the International Red Cross about the fate of those who went missing from prisons, we talk about notification from prison authorities, yes. At quite a large number of the working group sessions, reference was made to the fact that the representatives of the International Red Cross got lists from prison authorities in writing. It was not mentioned, though, who gave such a list to a delegate of the International Red Cross, whether this happened at the KP Dom Foca itself or some other place. It was mentioned that there was a list in writing through which the prison authorities were sending notification concerning the detainees mentioned in 240/7.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In relation to this particular list of 181 names, were you informed by the Red Cross whether or not they received that notification of the 181 names at one time, or over a period of time? Was it a wholesale notification of the 181 names, or were the notifications made at different times and then this document was compiled by the Red Cross? The question I have for you: Were you advised of when the notifications were made, were they made together or separately?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not the only document of such nature that we received from the International Committee of the Red Cross. We have received several such documents involving a smaller or a larger number of persons. I think that this document, 240/7, contains the largest number of persons so far about whom notification was sent by the prison authorities. I said already that we had received similar documents before, but there are quite a few documents that we have been receiving on a continuous basis from the International Committee of the Red Cross. You will see that this does not only include the Foca prison but also a series of other prisons, and the notifications were actually sent in over a longer period of time, not only in 1992, but that notification concerning some prisoners was sent in in 1993. And perhaps, yes, yes, perhaps even in 1994. Some of them in 1994, like prisoner 40, Dedic Amir, about whom notification was sent in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And his fate remains unknown.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If I can just stop you there. But were you told by the Red Cross when you received this document whether they received this notification of the 181 names at one time or separate times, or were you not told?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Are we really concerned with when the Red Cross received the notifications?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Just in relation to -- it's not of major importance but just in relation to perhaps typographical errors in relation to names and dates of birth. It might explain it a bit more, but ... All I need is an answer to the question, Your Honour, and then we can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Can you answer that question, Mr. Masovic?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is obviously a problem here, and that is why mistakes appear in the names of detainees and the years of their birth. The delegate of the Red Cross did not have access to the detainees themselves. Had the delegate had access, he would have registered the name and surname and year of birth properly, as well as all the other details concerning every detainee. The point here was that the prison authorities did not allow the delegate of the ICRC access to the detainees in prison, that they handed in their own list or perhaps even dictated a list to the representative of the International Red Cross, and in this specific case it is the 30th of August, 1992. So it was a list of detainees who were in prison then. As I said on several occasions, the International Red Cross gave us such lists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sir, we've got to stop the answer. We'll come back to it after the adjournment. But whilst we have this adjournment, the witness, next witness, [redacted], I think, has voice distortion. We would be grateful if that could be organised during the adjournment so we don't have to adjourn as soon as the witness arrives. We'll resume at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, in the speed that we adjourned for the break and the speed of the witness's answer, I didn't notice that he in fact answered the question which really was my last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You mean, what he was going on to say you didn't need?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, I'm afraid it was not the speed, it was the length of the answer. We do have certain obligations in relation to when we adjourn because of the court reporters and the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I apologise for missing that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Anyway, are we finished with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Perhaps just before the witness leaves, I would like to confirm that the request by the Trial Chamber as to identifying the sources of 240/5, they would be required in writing rather than the witness coming back to the Tribunal actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's what I had anticipated, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And that's the same with the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Witness, for giving your evidence. You're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour. If I can just mention one further matter. In relation to the two detainees that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Do you need the witness here for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No. Thanks, Mr. Masovic, you may leave, then. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In relation to the identifications of the two detainees that the Prosecution allege were exhumed, Halid Konjo and Obanjo [phoen] Konjo, I would just wonder if I can ask the Defence whether they still wish -- the Prosecution to produce the two witnesses that actually made the identification, the two family members, of the two bodies, or whether or not the evidence so far is enough in their view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, that's something which surely you can discuss between yourselves. They may want to consider the position, but if there's any problem, then you can raise it after a convenient adjournment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, while we're waiting for this witness with voice distortion to come along, we've discovered a new trap for using this particular courtroom, or a new problem with this courtroom. The system is not as well set up here for voice distortion as it is in the other courtrooms, so that for those who wish to hear the undistorted voice of the witness, you must go to channel 7; but if you want to hear the B/C/S version of anything said to the witness by the counsel, which will no doubt be in English, you have to swap to number 6. So it will be going from one -- either listening to the questions in English or you will be changing between 6 and 7 throughout the whole of this witness's evidence. I'm sorry for that. It may be another reason we can use to show that we are being discriminated against for having to use number 2 courtroom. The pseudonym document for Witness 249 will be Exhibit P440, and it is under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we start and everything is arranged, maybe we could already enter the transcript and some other documents into evidence. We had actually agreed, Defence counsels and the Prosecution had already agreed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is that in relation to this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, sit down for a moment, please, sir. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And it is actually the ID number in the binders, 158, which is the ICR certificate that is discussed in the transcript, and it is ID 159. This is an ICRC identity card. It is ID 160 and 160/A which is also a certificate about his exchange and detention. Then we have ID 161, which is actually the transcript from the previous testimony, and ID 161/1 would be the tapes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The videotapes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The videotapes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any objection to any of those, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Do any of those need to go in under seal? The first one obviously will.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. I think even the transcript because the transcript refers to the number, the previous number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well, then, all of those will be under seal, and they become exhibits P158, P159, P160, P160/A, P161, and P161/1. Now, we have the witness, please. Would you stand up, sir. And would you make the solemn declaration on the card which the usher is showing you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down please, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good morning, witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: Good morning. I can hear you well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, in front of you, you have a sheet of paper, and I have some -- several questions related to this sheet of paper. There is the witness number 249 on this sheet, and that's actually the number you are referred to in these proceedings; and below, you see a name. Is it your name?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the date underneath your name, is it your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Under your date of birth, there is the name of a person. Is it your son's name?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Underneath your son's name are listed a group of persons with the same last name. Are these relatives of you from Jelec?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When we speak about these persons during your testimony, you just refer to them here on the sheet of paper. Underneath these names you find four more names listed with pseudonym numbers or initials. These are actually protected witnesses, and if you want to refer to them in your testimony, please use their code numbers or initials. Witness, we do not need to repeat the evidence that you have already given in another trial. I would rather just ask you some additional questions. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. In relation to your stay in Jelec after the outbreak of the war, I have actually one question: During this time period, did the residents of Jelec organise village guards?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when did the villages keep guard; during daytime, nighttime, or both?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: Mostly during the night.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what were the guards supposed to do? Why were they there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: The role of the guards was to secure civilians at the given moment if there should be an attack, because almost everyone had packed their things should it become necessary for them to evacuate.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you participate in standing guard?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how often did you actually stand guard?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: Maybe a couple of times.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And just a completely unrelated question; do you know a person Enver Berber, father's name Tahir, from Jelec?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: I know Enver Berber. I believe Tahir Berber was his father.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see this person in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: I did see Enver. I think there was also a Mustafa Berber, his brother or cousin.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And are you able to tell us how old Enver Berber was, approximately? Was he an elderly person or was he a younger man at that time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: Enver Berber was the younger brother of this Mustafa Berber who was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And would you know his approximate age? I mean Enver's age.

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: At that time, he may have been 25, 26, maybe 27.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. In your previous testimony you told us that you were arrested on the 25th May, 1992, and that you were detained in Room 16.

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where in the building was Room 16?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: From the entrance, the metal door which led to the courtyard, the compound, you had to go 20 or 30 metres, then climb a flight of stairs, and then turn left at the landing, and that's where Room 16 was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So that means it's on the ground floor of the building number 2 of the prisoners' quarters?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: Yes, the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How long did you stay in this room; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: In Room 16, I stayed maybe 50 to 60 days.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know to which other rooms you were transferred?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: After a group of people was formed who were supposed to go to this forced labour, I was transferred to Room 18, but only for a few days before I was transferred to another wing of the same building.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And to which wing do you mean, to which room; do you know?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: The building itself was like the letter F, so we were in the middle part. That's where Room 16 and 18 were. And this other wing where we went to was slightly larger and longer.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to show the Witness the photo 7513. It's this. Please put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you see here the building number 2 where you said you were in 16 and 18, and can you now show us where you were transferred to when you were in this group of workers? You have to point at it on the ELMO, not on your screen.

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: That is Room 16, and the other wing is this one. I think we were here. I don't know the number of the room, I couldn't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness was pointing to building number 1 on the photo 7512, and he was pointing, if I -- and if I see it correctly, he's pointing to the second floor.

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In addition to the rooms, were you ever taken to solitary confinement cells?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: I was taken to solitary cells twice.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When were you taken -- when were you taken there for the first time and why?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: The first time I was taken to a solitary cell was after I went out for a snack. There were people there who didn't go out at all, and we sometimes left for them a piece of bread or something for them out of solidarity, and we would pass it to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, Witness, I hate to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This is finished. You can put IT off the ELMO, and you can also put off the photo. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So please continue.

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: So out of solidarity, we gave what we saved to people who cleaned the canteen to pass it to those who didn't go out at all, and thus I saved a piece of bread to be given to [redacted]-- I'm sorry, it's not [redacted]. I mean the surgeon. I can't recall -- Aziz. I wanted him to get this piece of bread, and my neighbour [redacted] saved a plum for him. And the guard on duty who was in the compound noticed that I had something in my pocket, and he asked my neighbour what it was, and this neighbour of mine, [redacted] who confessed immediately made no bones about it, was not punished by being sent to a solitary cell. He was returned to the metalwork shop where he usually worked, and I was sent to solitary confinement.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And who --

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: And sorry, the piece of bread I'd saved was for Dr. Aziz Torlak, the surgeon.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And who actually sent you to solitary confinement?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: It's a guard nicknamed Pedo whose full name I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in solitary confinement?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: I stayed in solitary confinement until that evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So does that mean you were released on that same day?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: Yes, on the same day, on the same evening I was released.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And who released you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: I was released by the second shift, which arrived in the afternoon, and every evening they counted us in our rooms. And when they noticed that one person is missing from my room, they asked who it was, and my mates from the room told them that I was missing and told them where I was, so they came to fetch me from the isolation cell.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that you were taken to the solitary confinement cell twice. The second time, is that in relation to the escape of Mr. Zekovic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We will talk about this somewhat later during your testimony. You testified previously that you had to work during your confinement in the KP Dom. When did you actually start working in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: My first job in the KP Dom was in the metalwork shop because by trade I am [redacted].

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when did you start to work, do you recall? Do you recall how much time you had already spent in the KP Dom when you started?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: I couldn't say exactly the date or even the days I spent in individual rooms, but I believe it was around 40 days after I was taken into custody.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You called it forced labour. Were you forced to work, or did you work voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: No doubt it was forced labour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Why do you say that? What -- who forced you to work?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: The first time I went out of the KP Dom was when the guard who was in the courtyard came with a piece of paper and called out my name, and my name was not -- was not written there quite correctly. And then he came back again and called me out again, pronouncing my name properly, and then I was taken out.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did other detainees start to work before you did, or were you actually the first, in the first group?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: No. A couple of men had already started to work in the metalwork shop. Sevko Kubat, Suad Islambasic, and Karahasanovic were among them. That's about the car repair shop where I was taken to work. These people I've mentioned had gone to work before I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did other detainees start to work while you were already working, that means after you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned those who have already started to work before you, and then you said you were called out after about 40 days. Did other detainees have to start working after you, that is, did they start to work later than you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: There were many others who started coming to the metalwork shop to work after me.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How many detainees actually were in this group of workers altogether?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: It's difficult to say, at least speaking about the metalwork shop itself, because it depended on the requirements, on the job in question. Some people came to work for a while, then they would leave. And there was a permanent group of metal workers who were metal workers by occupation; lathe operators, welders, locksmiths. That was a permanent group, and this group never changed. And in addition to them, there was some other people who came from time to time to clean, to do a painting job, and that was the changing group.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The permanent group, how many people were they?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: Well, this permanent group consisted of about 10 to 12 people, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: All working in the metalwork shop?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what about the other facilities where work was conducted, when you put together -- when you count also these detainees who worked in other facilities, how many were there altogether? The entire working platoon, how many were they?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: You mean forced labour?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: I don't know. It's difficult to say because there were groups and groups. You could never tell. People would often get sick from the food they would get in the evening. They would have diarrhea during the night, lose a lot of fluid, and would be unable to go to work in the morning, so this number always varied. There were people who went to the mine, who went to Kosovina, to the farm. Some of them went to cut grass. So I cannot really say how many people there were in each group.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said earlier that you were in a particular room, kept this working room. That's, at least, what I understood. You were kept in a particular room in the building number 1 on the second floor. How many detainees were in this particular room?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: The working platoon was already formed and people went to various locations. There were metal workers, people who worked on the farm, people who cut grass, and that was when the working platoon was already established at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Would you be able to estimate the number of detainees who were permanently working? If you can't, just say, "I can't."

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: I don't think I can tell you the figure.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned that in the metalwork shop there were people with -- workers with special skills. You mentioned welders and others. Was the prison administration aware of the skills of the detainees?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: I think they were. At the outset, it may be a coincidence, I don't know, but they really took out people who had some skills. I don't know where they got their information, but the people who were taken out knew how to do the job.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What happened when you were taken out for the first time? You have already mentioned that a guard called you out, and what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: I was first taken to the metalwork shop, and as soon as I got there I saw my neighbour, Relja Goljanin. There was also a person nicknamed Dule, and people who been taken out before.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to have the steps that were taken more detailed. The guard who took you out from your room, where did he go with you within the compound of the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: He took me outside the compound through the metal door and straight to the metalwork shop.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to show the witness the photo 7470. It's the bottom photo.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, when you look at the photo, at the lower photo, what -- do you recognise what kind of room it is?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: Yes. That's the transit room from which you enter the compound of the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Is the arrow pointing at the metal door that you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: Yes, that's it precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you had passed this metal door, were you received by any person in this passage room, as you called it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: At the very entrance from the compound, there was always a guard on duty who received us immediately. He always counted the people who were going out and wrote down the number in his register at the desk, and here you see the desk.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness was pointing at the desk right -- left, left to the yellow arrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The guard who was making those notification, into what did he write who was going where? Did he have a kind of a book, or did he have a list?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249
utterances.text: He had a book. If somebody was taken to the metal shop, then they would know who was taken to the metal shop. Records were kept in that book. Also, upon returning, on the basis of the number that was recorded in that book, people were sent back into the KP Dom compound.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
